name: Centurion

location.address: Arve Valley, Tall Trees area off Arve Road, south of Geeveston, Huon Valley, Tasmania
location.neighbourhood: Geeveston / Arve Valley (day trip from Hobart)

access: Free, no permission needed; a state forest reserve reached via a rough but 2WD-passable forestry road (Arve Road/Edwards Link Road) and then an unmarked, muddy, self-guided walking track through rainforest. No gate, booking or ticket, but genuinely remote: no mobile phone coverage, and access roads sit inside an active logging area and can close without notice.
transport: No public transport reaches it. Roughly 1.5 to 2 hours' drive south of Hobart via the Huon Highway to Geeveston, then forestry roads; the final stretch is on foot. An honest day trip by car, not a walk from town.
story:
Australia's tallest tree was found by a computer. In August 2008 Forestry Tasmania staff running LiDAR over state forest in the Arve Valley picked out a return that should not have been there, walked in, and found a mountain ash within a whisker of a hundred metres tall. It was the hundredth notable tree they had catalogued, which is where the name came from. For a while they also called it the Bradman, because an early tape-drop of 99.82 metres landed close to Don Bradman's Test batting average.

The measurements have wandered ever since: 99.6 metres by tape in 2008, 99.82 in 2014, a lower 99.67 in 2016, and a laser-measured 100.5 metres in December 2018. Then the 2019 Tasmanian bushfires came through. Centurion survived with a new hollow burned into its base. A neighbouring giant called the Prefect, nineteen metres round, did not. By 2025 the tree was reported at 96 metres, four metres shorter, still alive and still growing.

No age has ever been published for it. Getting there is a genuine expedition: an hour and a half to two hours south of Hobart by car, forestry roads through an active logging area that can close without warning, then an unmarked muddy track through rainforest with no phone signal at any point.

name: Bland Oak

location.address: Oakdene Park, Bland Street, Carramar NSW 2163
location.neighbourhood: Carramar, City of Fairfield, Greater Western Sydney

access: Free, public council park (Oakdene Park), open at all times, no restrictions.
transport: Carramar railway station (Sydney Trains T5 Cumberland Line) is close by; roughly 45-60 minutes by train from central Sydney.
story:
On New Year's Day 1941 a storm split what was reported to be the largest tree in Australia into two pieces. The salvaged timber was carved into Fairfield's mayoral chair, now held at the city's museum, and the oak itself is still alive in Oakdene Park.

William Bland planted it in 1842. He arrived in New South Wales as a convict and became one of colonial Sydney's more prominent figures, a surgeon, a politician, a farmer and an inventor. What he put in the ground was a southern live oak, an American species, and 1842 is a documented planting date rather than an estimate, which gives this tree one of the few real birthdays in Sydney: 184 years.

It never recovered the size it lost in 1941 and it is still the largest oak of its kind in the city, about thirteen metres tall with a canopy spreading more than thirty metres across. Fairfield put it on the city's coat of arms. The National Trust added it to the National Register of Significant Trees in 2018, and in 2020 the council germinated acorns from it to raise about ten young Bland Oaks around the district, which is the most practical answer anyone has found to a tree that cannot last forever.

Oakdene Park is free and open at any hour. Carramar station is a short walk, 45 to 60 minutes by train from central Sydney.

name: Gregory's Tree

location.address: Gregory's Tree Historical Reserve, 1740 Victoria Hwy, Gregory NT (15km north-west of Timber Creek, within Judbarra / Gregory National Park)
location.neighbourhood: Timber Creek, Victoria River District, Northern Territory

access: Free, public historical reserve beside the Victoria Highway; a marked track leads from a roadside cairn to the tree, which has its own boardwalk and interpretative panels built around it. It is also a registered Aboriginal sacred site to the Ngaringman people (who know it as Ngalibinggag), so the public boardwalk keeps visitors from touching or approaching the trunk directly; this does not restrict viewing.
transport: No public transport; self-drive only, on the Victoria Highway roughly 15km north-west of Timber Creek, NT, and about 3.5 hours' drive west of Katherine.
story:
This boab carries two dates cut into its bark: 13 October 1855 and 2 July 1856, the arrival and the departure of Augustus Charles Gregory's North Australia Expedition, which made its entrenchment camp beside the Victoria River here. The carvings are still readable.

The expedition's botanist was Ferdinand von Mueller, who became one of the most consequential botanists in Australian history, and who named the Australian boab Adansonia gregorii after the man leading the party. So the tree belongs to a species named for the expedition that carved it. That is a rarer credential than any age figure.

Nobody has published an age for it, and boabs are notoriously hard to date. The Northern Territory Heritage Register, which permanently declared the place in 1995, settles for calling it a living monument to the exploration of northern Australia.

It is also Ngalibinggag, a registered sacred site of the Ngaringman people, and the reserve is built around that: a boardwalk and interpretive panels ring the tree so that visitors keep off the ground at its base and do not touch the trunk. Looking is the whole visit, and nothing about the looking is restricted.

The reserve sits on the Victoria Highway about fifteen kilometres north-west of Timber Creek, three and a half hours' drive west of Katherine, with no public transport of any kind. Come in the dry.

best_time.label: the dry season, when the leaves are off and the carved trunk is the whole tree
